n: God answers the people’s confession: if you truly return and remove your detestable idols, you won’t have to wander into exile.

f.w: If thou wilt return, O Israel

f.g: Wander—be driven from the land.

n: If you swear “As the Lord lives” with truth, justice, and righteousness, then the nations will be blessed through Him—fulfilling God’s promise to Abraham.

f.w: the nations shall bless themselves in him

n: An agricultural image: plow up your hard, unused ground and don’t sow among thorns. Prepare your hearts before trying to grow anything good.

f.g: Plow hard, unplowed soil—make your hearts soft and ready.

n: Circumcise your hearts. Physical circumcision was the sign of the covenant; God wants inner commitment—hearts cut free from sin—or His anger will burn like unquenchable fire.

f.w: take away the foreskins of your heart

n: Sound the alarm! Blow the trumpet across the land and tell people to flee to the fortified cities.

f.g: Fortified, walled towns.

n: Raise a signal flag toward Zion; run for safety and don’t delay! God is bringing disaster from the north.

f.g: Raise a signal pole to direct refugees.

f.w: I will bring evil from the north

n: A lion has come out of its thicket—a destroyer of nations is on the move to devastate Judah. The lion represents Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar.

f.w: The lion is come up from his thicket

f.g: The destroyer of nations.

n: So put on sackcloth, mourn, and wail—the Lord’s fierce anger has not turned away.

f.g: Wear rough goat-hair cloth—a sign of mourning.

n: On that day the king and officials will lose courage, the priests will be horrified, and the prophets stunned. The leaders who promised safety will be paralyzed.

f.w: the heart of the king shall perish

n: Jeremiah cries out in anguish: Lord, You’ve let this people be deceived by promises of peace, but the sword is at their throat! The false prophets had promised peace, and God allowed the deception they wanted to hear.

f.w: surely thou hast greatly deceived this people
f.g: A lament: God permitted false prophets’ comforting lies.

n: A scorching wind from the desert heights is blowing toward the people—not the gentle breeze used to winnow grain, but a destructive blast.

f.w: not to fan, nor to cleanse
f.g: Not a winnowing breeze that separates chaff, but a hot, destructive wind (the sirocco).

n: This wind is too strong for winnowing; it comes at God’s command as He pronounces judgment.
Look! The enemy rises like storm clouds, chariots like a whirlwind, horses faster than eagles. “Woe to us—we are ruined!”

f.w: his horses are swifter than eagles

f.g: Plundered, devastated.

n: Jerusalem, wash the evil from your heart so you can be saved. How long will you harbor wicked thoughts? Even at the last moment, repentance is possible.

f.g: Wicked or worthless thoughts.

n: A messenger announces disaster from Dan in the far north and then from the hills of Ephraim, closer to Jerusalem. The news travels south as the invader approaches.

f.g: Israel’s northernmost city.
The hill country just north of Jerusalem.

n: Announce to the nations: besiegers are coming from a distant land, shouting war cries against Judah’s cities.

f.g: Besiegers, those who surround a city.

n: Like guards around a field, they surround Jerusalem—because she rebelled against God.
Your own behavior brought this on you. This is the bitter fruit of your wickedness, and it pierces to your heart.

f.w: Thy way and thy doings have procured these things

n: Jeremiah cries out in physical pain: “My anguish, my anguish! My heart is pounding—I can’t keep quiet!” He hears the war trumpet in his soul. Jeremiah is often called the “weeping prophet.”

f.g: My insides, my deepest feelings—the seat of emotion in Hebrew thought.

n: Disaster after disaster—the whole land is ruined. Suddenly the tents are destroyed, the curtains torn down in a moment.

f.g: Homes—Jeremiah speaks for the whole people.

n: How long must I see the battle flag and hear the trumpet?
God explains: My people are foolish. They don’t know Me. They are clever at doing evil but have no idea how to do good.

f.g: Stupid, senseless.

f.w: they are wise to do evil

n: Jeremiah sees a vision of creation undone: the earth “without form and void” and the sky dark—the same words as Genesis 1:2. Sin is pictured as reversing creation.

f.g: Hebrew tohu va-bohu—the phrase used for the earth before creation.

n: Mountains quake and hills sway—the stable world shaken.

f.w: the mountains, and, lo, they trembled

n: No people anywhere, and even the birds have fled. Creation’s final works—humans and birds—are gone.
The fertile land has become desert and its cities lie in ruins before the Lord’s fierce anger. A garden turned back to wilderness.

f.g: Hebrew Carmel—the garden land.

n: Yet a glimmer of mercy: the whole land will be desolate, but God will not make a complete end. A remnant will survive.

f.w: yet will I not make a full end

n: The earth mourns and the heavens grow dark, because God has spoken and will not change His decision.

f.g: Will not change My mind or relent.

n: At the sound of horsemen and archers, every town empties; people hide in thickets and climb among rocks.
Jerusalem is pictured as a woman dressing in scarlet, gold jewelry, and eye makeup to win over her lovers (foreign allies). It’s useless—those lovers despise her and want her dead.

f.g: Enlarge your eyes with dark eye paint (kohl).

n: Jeremiah hears a cry like a woman in labor with her first child—Zion gasping, stretching out her hands: “Woe is me! I’m fainting before murderers.”

f.g: Stretching out hands in helpless pleading.
